facilities.name: Sabey Data Centers Ashburn - Building A

source.basis: Operator facility page; structured facts only, no operator prose reproduced.

profile.reading:
Sabey Data Centers' SDC Ashburn campus sits in Loudoun County's "Data Center Alley," with this building, Building A, at 21735 Red Rum Drive, Ashburn, Virginia, per OpenStreetMap address data corroborated against the operator's own Ashburn location page. Sabey is one of seven data center campuses the company operates nationally as of 2026. Sabey traces its roots to 1972, when Dave Sabey founded Sabey Corporation as a Pacific Northwest commercial real estate developer; the company entered the data center business almost by accident during the dot-com collapse, when a vacated tenant building in Seattle became SDC Seattle Building 5. Sabey Data Centers itself was formally established in 2010 as a joint venture between Sabey Corporation and institutional investor National Real Estate Advisors, a structure confirmed on both the operator's own site and independently by Wikipedia.

Building A sits alongside neighboring Buildings B (21745 Red Rum Drive) and C (21741 Red Rum Drive) on the same Red Rum Drive block. Per Wikipedia's most recent coverage of the company, the Ashburn campus has grown to include a third building under construction, with roughly 85 MW of total planned campus capacity once complete, though that figure is not broken out per building and is not assigned to this structure specifically. Sabey markets its data center facilities, including Ashburn, as carrying SOC 1 Type 2, SOC 2 Type 2, PCI DSS, HIPAA, ISO 27001, and SSAE 18 compliance attestations, per the operator's own site; those attestations describe compliance posture rather than physical capacity.

Sabey's national footprint as of this writing spans Seattle and the Columbia River region (Quincy and East Wenatchee, Washington, powered by hydroelectricity), Ashburn, Manhattan (Intergate Manhattan at 375 Pearl Street, opened 2013 in a retrofitted former Verizon/NY Telephone switching building), the Austin, Texas metro area (a first Round Rock building completed October 2024), and a planned Umatilla, Oregon campus exceeding 100 MW. Tim Mirick became Sabey's president effective January 1, 2025, succeeding Rob Rockwood, per Wikipedia. No building-specific opening date, individual power capacity, or technical/building square footage figure for this Ashburn building has been located in operator or public sourcing to date; that gap is noted honestly rather than estimated, and the previously recorded 54 MW figure on this row has been removed as unconfirmed at the building level (it duplicated the operator's separate, campus-wide Seattle capacity figure and does not describe this Virginia building).
profile.research_note: Sabey publishes campus-level totals only for SDC Ashburn (85 MW capacity, 645k sqft mission-critical space, >100 kW/rack capability) not broken out per building (A/B/C), so left out of it_capacity_mw/technical_space_sqft. Building A is future/not yet online (54MW additional capacity expected starting 2026).

profile.reading:
Sabey Data Centers operates the Intergate.Columbia campus at 4405 Grant Road in East Wenatchee, Douglas County, Washington, along the Columbia River in central Washington state. Sabey Corporation was founded in 1972 by Dave Sabey as a Pacific Northwest commercial real estate developer, and the company entered the data center business around 2010 when a large tenant vacated a Seattle building during the dot-com era downturn, leaving behind space that became SDC Seattle Building 5. Sabey Data Centers was formally established that same year as a partnership between Sabey Corporation and institutional investor National Real Estate Advisors. The company's own site currently lists seven operating campuses, SDC Ashburn, SDC Austin, SDC Columbia, SDC Manhattan, SDC Quincy, SDC Seattle, and SDC Umatilla, together totaling more than 3.5 million square feet, with additional projects described by the company as in development.

Per Sabey's own SDC Columbia campus page, the East Wenatchee site runs on hydroelectric power supplied by Douglas County Public Utility District, priced at 5 cents per kilowatt hour, among the lowest electricity rates available to data center operators anywhere in the country. Douglas County PUD draws its hydroelectric generation from Columbia River dams the utility operates, the same regional low-cost hydropower base that has also drawn data center investment to nearby Quincy and other mid-Columbia sites operated by other companies. The Intergate.Columbia campus comprises three completed buildings and a fourth under construction, with 70 megawatts currently under power campus-wide and, per the operator, more than 90 additional megawatts of capacity coming as buildout continues, a total Sabey does not break down building by building. Sabey markets the campus at an average annualized power usage effectiveness of about 1.2, and states its ENERGY STAR score has consistently ranked in the 95th to 100th percentile among comparable buildings, most recently a 99 for 2024. The campus holds ISO 27001 certification, SSAE 18 SOC 1 Type 2 and SOC 2 Type 2 attestations, and is described by the operator as HIPAA, HITECH, and PCI DSS compliant, with connections to more than seven Tier 1 network carriers including AT&T, Verizon, Charter Spectrum, Zayo, and Ziply Fiber. Sabey describes the facility's reliability design as Tier III standard equivalent, backed by 2.75 megawatt backup generators rated for 72 hours of runtime.

This registry entry tracks the Intergate.Columbia campus generally rather than one numbered building, since this registry separately carries building level entries for Buildings A, B, and D at or near the same Grant Road address. No individual building capacity or square footage figure is published by the operator for any single building on this campus, only the campus-wide totals above.

profile.reading:
Intergate Seattle East Building 1 is part of Sabey Data Centers' Tukwila, Washington campus, which Sabey markets today as a single site called SDC Seattle, a few miles south of downtown Seattle and about three miles from Sea-Tac International Airport. Building 1 sits in the cluster of buildings along South 120th Place that Sabey and public mapping data still refer to as the Intergate.East side of the site, alongside Building 2 at 3311 South 120th Place and Building 3 at 3333 South 120th Place. No street address specific to Building 1 was found in this pass, only its coordinates placing it a short distance from those two neighboring buildings on the same block.

Sabey Data Centers is the data center subsidiary of Sabey Corporation, a Puget Sound commercial real estate and construction company founded in 1972 by Dave Sabey that built its early business as a major industrial and office landlord in the Seattle area through the aerospace driven growth of the 1970s and 1980s. Sabey's own company history describes its move into data centers as tracing back to a tenant vacating one of its buildings during the dot com collapse of the early 2000s, leaving Sabey with an empty large scale technical shell, now counted as SDC Seattle Building 5, that the company recognized as an opportunity in a market starting to demand purpose built computing space. Sabey formalized that pivot in 2010 by partnering with institutional investor National Real Estate Advisors to create Sabey Data Centers as a dedicated operating company, which today describes its national portfolio as more than four million square feet of mission critical space across six campuses in Washington, New York, Texas, and Virginia, with more in development.

On power and scale, Sabey's own site describes SDC Seattle as a whole running on hydroelectric power delivered by Seattle City Light, with more than 90 MVA of aggregate utility power delivered to the campus through redundant feeds, backup generators rated at 2.5 MW apiece with 72 hour runtime at peak load, about 9,500 tons of installed HVAC capacity, and over a million square feet of total space. These figures describe the entire Tukwila site, covering both the Intergate.East cluster where Building 1 sits and the separate Intergate.West cluster of buildings on Tukwila International Boulevard, not any single building within it, and Sabey does not publish a building level IT load, utility power, or generator count specific to Building 1. Sabey's certifications for the SDC Seattle campus as a whole include HIPAA and HITECH alignment, PCI DSS, SSAE 18 SOC 1 Type 2 and SOC 2 Type 2, LEED Gold, and ISO 27001, again applied at the campus level rather than to individual buildings.

No King County Assessor parcel record, City of Tukwila building permit, or construction and occupancy date specific to Building 1 was identified in this pass, and no trade press coverage naming this building individually, as opposed to the SDC Seattle campus as a whole, was found either.

profile.reading:
Intergate Seattle East Building 2 sits on Sabey Data Centers' SDC Seattle campus at 3311 South 120th Place in Tukwila, King County, Washington, a few miles south of downtown Seattle and about three miles from Sea-Tac International Airport. The operator is Sabey Data Centers, the data center arm of Sabey Corporation, a Puget Sound commercial real estate and construction company founded in 1972 by Dave Sabey. Sabey Corporation grew into one of Boeing's largest landlords during the aerospace boom of the 1970s and 1980s, and in the mid 1990s it developed the Intergate East and West campuses in Tukwila for technology tenants, sites that already carried unusually heavy electrical infrastructure, two power stations that had originally served steel mills in the area, a legacy of industrial capacity that made Tukwila attractive once demand shifted toward computing. Sabey's own published history and a 2025 Data Center Dynamics report both describe the East campus as a six building complex that Sabey originally developed, that Boeing purchased around 1990, and that Sabey reacquired in 1999 as it pivoted toward data centers following the dot com collapse, a pivot Sabey Corporation formalized in 2010 when it partnered with institutional investor National Real Estate Advisors to create the present day Sabey Data Centers company. Tim Mirick became president of Sabey Data Centers effective January 1, 2025, succeeding Rob Rockwood after his eight years in the role, and the company describes its current national portfolio as more than four million square feet of mission critical space, among the largest privately owned multi tenant data center operators in the country.

Location here is also a Pacific Northwest power story. Sabey's own materials describe the Seattle campus as running on hydroelectric power delivered by Seattle City Light, drawing on the same abundant, low carbon hydro generation from the region's dammed rivers that has long made western Washington attractive to power hungry industrial and computing tenants, distinct from but related to the cheaper Columbia River hydro power that has separately drawn large scale computing to central Washington.

On scale and power, the 2025 Data Center Dynamics report describes the Seattle campus as totaling 54 MW of capacity across roughly 1.2 million square feet spanning its multiple buildings, with an additional 6 MW of liquid cooling ready, Tier III standard critical power the operator said was scheduled to come online by December 1, 2025. Sabey's own site separately describes campus wide infrastructure of more than 90 MVA of aggregate utility power delivered through redundant feeds and backup generators rated 2.5 MW apiece with 72 hour runtime at peak load. These are campus wide figures spanning all buildings on the site, not numbers specific to Building 2, and no IT load, utility service, or standby generation figure specific to this individual building was found in public sourcing, so none is recorded here.

reading:
Sabey Data Centers is a privately held, family-owned operator headquartered in the Seattle, Washington area. Its parent, Sabey Corporation, was established in 1972 by Dave Sabey, and Sabey Data Centers itself formed in 2010 as a partnership between Sabey Corporation and National Real Estate Advisors.

The company's own site describes a portfolio of six data center campuses, with more in development, spanning its original Pacific Northwest base in Seattle and the broader Puget Sound area, plus Columbia near East Wenatchee, Quincy, and Umatilla, Oregon, alongside campuses in Ashburn, Virginia, Austin, Texas, and Manhattan, New York. No precise total capacity figure in megawatts or square footage was located on the operator's site this session.

The registry here tracks 12 Sabey facilities across two states, Virginia and Washington, a narrower footprint than the seven-market list on the operator's own site, which additionally names Texas, New York, and Oregon locations. As one of the smaller family-owned operators in this registry, alongside CloudHQ's Fateh Family Office structure, Sabey's Quincy and East Wenatchee campuses sit in Washington's Columbia River hydropower corridor, a low-cost power region distinct from the AWS, Meta, and Google buildouts concentrated in Oregon's Columbia River sites tracked elsewhere in this registry.
